39.0.0.en: This chapter tells us how Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem. In this verse it declares that the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar began in the tenth month of the ninth year of King Zedekiah, which is in the year 588 BC.

39.1.0.en: The Babylonian siege of Jerusalem continued from January of the year 588 BC until the summer of the same year, when they were forced to lift the siege for a short time because of the movement of the army of Egypt. Then Nebuchadnezzar triumphed over Egypt in the battle of Carchemish in Iraq, and after that Nebuchadnezzar returned and besieged Jerusalem, which had become very weak from hunger, thirst and disease, and he entered it and took it in the summer of the year 587 BC, in the month of July, that is, about a year and a half after the beginning of the siege. This was in the fourth month of the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.

39.2.0.en: The middle gate: probably the main gate of Jerusalem, which was built on five hills, the most important of which were a hill in the north and another in the south with a deep valley between them. This gate led to this valley, which divides the city into two parts, so it is called the middle gate. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard who led the army, attacked the city of Jerusalem and stormed it, and the princes of the army of Babylon entered and sat in the main gate of the city of Jerusalem, declaring their capture of this city. They did not enter into its depths lest harm come to them from one of the people, but the soldiers of Babylon moved to seize whomever they wished throughout the city, and they took the best of the people captive to Babylon. As for King Nebuchadnezzar, he waited in the city of Riblah to prevent any forces coming to the aid of Jerusalem. The princes mentioned here are some of the princes who entered Jerusalem and not all of them, and the functions of some are mentioned: one of them was the chief of the eunuchs, who work as servants for the king of Babylon, and another was the chief of the magi, that is, the wise men and counselors of the king of Babylon. Other names of the princes are mentioned in (v. 13).

39.3.0.en: The king's garden: large gardens belonging to King Zedekiah beside the pool of Siloam.

39.3.1.en: The gate betwixt the two walls: a gate of Jerusalem lying on its south side. The plain: the deep valley of the Jordan north of the Dead Sea, which leads to the Arabian desert near Egypt.

39.3.2.en: When King Zedekiah saw the Babylonian forces beginning to enter Jerusalem, he hurried to flee, he and the men of war, that is, his special guard and the commanders of the army. They took cover by night so that no one would see them, and went out by the way of the king's garden to one of the gates of Jerusalem that lies in its south and is called the gate betwixt the two walls, which leads to the valley of the plain, from which they could flee to Egypt and take refuge in it.

39.4.0.en: The plains of Jericho: the plains of Jericho extending between Jericho and the river Jordan and also extending south as far as Jerusalem.

39.4.1.en: Riblah: a city lying in the land of Hamath, north of the city of Damascus, the capital of Syria.

39.4.2.en: While King Zedekiah and his fighting men were fleeing from Jerusalem in the plains of Jericho, the eyes of the king of Babylon were watching them and searching for them. They learned of their flight and pursued them until they overtook them, and seized them in these plains beside the river Jordan, and took them to Nebuchadnezzar, who was staying in the city of Riblah, which he had taken before.

39.5.0.en: Nebuchadnezzar commanded the killing of Zedekiah's sons, whom his men had seized with their father, and they killed them before Zedekiah's eyes to humiliate him and frighten him. Then he also commanded, and they killed the nobles of the kingdom of Judah who had been fleeing with Zedekiah. Thus Zedekiah felt complete helplessness after the killing of his children, his nobles and the fighters who defended him.

39.6.0.en: Nebuchadnezzar also commanded that Zedekiah's eyes be put out, in vengeance on him for not submitting, then bound him with fetters of brass, that is, very strong, from which he could not free himself, and they led him away captive to live as a captive in Babylon after he had lost all his strength and even his sight.

39.6.1.en: Do not rely on your strength and capabilities, nor on the opinions of people, for they are all weak and cannot protect you. Rather obey God and hold fast to His commandments, even if they seem heavy, trusting in His ability to help you, protect you and save you from every evil.

39.7.0.en: After they had killed the leaders of the kingdom of Judah and taken the rest of them captive, Jerusalem was left without a force to defend it, and this was about a month after its capture. Here Nebuchadnezzar commanded the burning of the king's palace and likewise the palaces of Jerusalem, so as to humiliate the city and leave it destroyed.

39.8.0.en: That fell to him: they fled and surrendered themselves to the armies of Babylon. The captain of the guard: the one responsible for security in Babylon. After that the armies of Babylon seized all the Jews fit for work, and also those who had fled from Jerusalem and surrendered themselves to the armies of Babylon, and took them captive, bound as slaves, to Babylon. All this was by the command of the commander of the Babylonian armies, Nebuzaradan.

39.9.0.en: Nothing remained in Jerusalem but the poor and weak of the Jews, and Nebuzaradan gave them the fields around Jerusalem to cultivate. He intended by this:

39.9.1.en: 1- To preserve these fields so that the Babylonians could take from them and make use of them when they wished in the form of taxes.

39.9.2.en: 2- That there should be in Jerusalem only the weak, unable to resist Babylon.

39.9.3.en: 3- To honor these poor, whom the nobles and rich of the Jews had exploited, and by this to win them over so that they owe loyalty to Babylon and not to their homeland.

39.10.0.en: These two verses make clear that “Nebuchadnezzar” charged the commander of his armies, Nebuzaradan, to release Jeremiah, care for him and give him the freedom to do what he wished, that is, complete freedom.

39.10.1.en: It is understood from this that Nebuzaradan brought him out of the prison in which King “Zedekiah” had imprisoned him and gave him his freedom in Jerusalem. But on referring to (Jer 40:1-2) we find that Jeremiah had been seized and taken captive to Babylon, and on the way, at a city called Ramah, the command came from Nebuchadnezzar to Nebuzaradan to release him and return him to Jerusalem a free man. There is no contradiction between the two chapters, for they brought him out of his prison and sent him to Babylon with the captives, but it appears that news reached Nebuchadnezzar from the captive Jews that Jeremiah was the prophet of God who had been calling the king and the people to submit to Babylon. So Nebuchadnezzar felt that he was not an enemy of his and released him and honored him as mentioned in this chapter, and he returned from Ramah to Jerusalem.

39.11.0.en: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan: he was cooperative with the Babylonians, who afterward appointed him governor over Jerusalem and its surroundings.

39.11.1.en: Nebuzaradan and the princes of Babylon carried out the commands of King Nebuchadnezzar and released Jeremiah from the prison, and handed him over to Gedaliah, who was to become governor over Jerusalem, to care for him and settle him among the people in Jerusalem, and to move about with complete freedom.

39.11.2.en: God cares for His children even in the hardest afflictions, and uses for this every means, even the enemies themselves. So do not be troubled however hard your circumstances, because God is with you, upholding you and delivering you from all dangers, and even caring for you so that you live with Him in reassurance.

39.11.4.en: 15- Now the word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah, while he was shut up in the court of the prison, saying, 16- Go and speak to Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring my words upon this city for evil, and not for good; and they shall be accomplished in that day before thee. 17- But I will deliver thee in that day, saith the LORD: and thou shalt not be given into the hand of the men of whom thou art afraid. 18- For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.

39.12.0.en: This goes back to mention a prophecy that God gave Jeremiah when he was imprisoned in Jerusalem, before Nebuzaradan released him.

39.13.0.en: God sent this prophecy by the mouth of Jeremiah to “Ebedmelech the Ethiopian,” one of the servants of “Zedekiah” king of Judah, among the counselors close to him, who had done a kindness to Jeremiah when he interceded for him before Zedekiah so that he would not die in the cistern full of mire, not afraid of the princes of the king of Judah who had put him in the cistern. He took a command from Zedekiah and brought Jeremiah out of the cistern and put him in a better prison (ch. 38:7-13). This divine message to Ebedmelech declares that God's word, of the destruction of Jerusalem and the killing and captivity of those in it, would be fulfilled quickly and “Ebedmelech” would see it.

39.14.0.en: This message also contained good news for Ebedmelech that God would deliver him from the hand of his Babylonian enemies so that they would not seize him.

39.15.0.en: The third matter that this message contained is that God would deliver him from death so that the Babylonians would not kill him, and this was because of his faith in God and his trust in Him, for he feared God and took pity on His prophet Jeremiah and rescued him from death, so God delivers him from death. Thus God preserved three:

39.15.1.en: (1) His prophet “Jeremiah,” because of his obedience to God and his proclaiming His voice to all the people.

39.15.2.en: (2) “Ebedmelech,” who represents the Gentiles who fear God and do mercy.

39.15.3.en: (3) The poor of the Jews to whom the Babylonians gave the fields and vineyards to cultivate and eat from, who represent the weak who rely on God.

39.15.4.en: If you obey God and fear Him and rely on Him, God will keep you and deliver you from evil, not only in this life but He will give you the glories of eternal life. So hold fast to God's commandments even if everyone keeps away from them, and do not forget your only goal, which is “the love of God.”

40.0.0.en: Ramah: a city lying 6 miles north of Jerusalem and 2 miles south-west of Mizpah. Perhaps what is meant by the word of God to Jeremiah is the decision of Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of the kingdom of Babylon, to release Jeremiah and his return to the captivity, to Mizpah, since he was among the captives whom the Babylonians took from Jerusalem and walked with toward Ramah. Orders came from Nebuchadnezzar to Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, to release Jeremiah, perhaps because he had heard from the Jews of Jeremiah's prophecies calling for submission to the king of Babylon, so he regarded him as a friend and not an enemy. This was by the provision of God to free Jeremiah.

40.1.0.en: Nebuzaradan uttered an important spiritual truth, namely that the destruction of Jerusalem was because of the Jews' disobedience to God's commandments. Perhaps this idea helped the Babylonians to destroy Jerusalem, but sadly the Jews did not understand this truth.

40.1.1.en: Take care lest the people of the world know spiritual truths that you do not know, just as Christ in the parable of the unjust steward asked us to learn wisdom from the children of this age. In proportion as you are submissive to God in prayer, He will guide you even through the mouths of the people of the world and not only through the mouths of the spiritual teachers in the Church.

40.2.0.en: Nebuzaradan issued an order to release Jeremiah, then left to him the choice of the place where he would stay, which was:

40.2.1.en: 1- Going to Babylon, where care and attention from Nebuzaradan awaited him.

40.2.2.en: 2- Going to any place he chose in the world.

40.3.0.en: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan: “Shaphan” was the official scribe of King Josiah and shared with him in the religious reforms, so he was a pious man, and his son “Ahikam” is “Gemariah,” one of the princes of King Jehoiakim, who feared God and tried to prevent the king from tearing up Jeremiah's prophecies (Jer 36:25). So Gedaliah was from a pious family, and his name is a Hebrew word meaning “Jehovah is great.” Nebuchadnezzar had appointed him as his deputy and governor of the kingdom of Judah after he took it.

40.3.1.en: Mizpah: it is eight miles from Jerusalem to its north-west, and very close to Ramah, so it was easy for Jeremiah to return to Mizpah, where Gedaliah the governor was. It is clear that Mizpah had not been destroyed by Babylon like Jerusalem.

40.3.2.en: Before Jeremiah decided where to stay, Nebuzaradan continued his talk with Jeremiah and said to him: go to Gedaliah, who is the governor of Judah, and he will care for you and you will stay among the people there. So Jeremiah obeyed and returned to Mizpah to live among his poor and weak people, after Nebuzaradan gave him a gift and provisions for the road and took care of him.

40.4.0.en: When Babylon attacked the kingdom of Judah, a large number of Jews fled to the surrounding mountains, such as the Ammonites, Moab and Edom. After the destruction of Jerusalem and many lands around it and Babylon's capture of the kingdom of Judah, it appointed Gedaliah governor over it to pay tribute to it. When the leading men among the Jews, who were probably soldiers, heard of what had happened, they returned to the land of Judah. It calls them the princes because they were strong and not like the weak who remained in Judah. It mentions some of them, such as Ishmael, who had fled to the land of the Ammonites and was a wicked man and made a pact with the king of the Ammonites to take the kingdom of Judah. It also mentions two pious brothers, Johanan and Jonathan, sons of Kareah, and others.

40.5.0.en: Gedaliah was affected by the word of God through the mouth of Jeremiah, so when he received these princes mentioned in (v. 8) he said to them: submit to the king of Babylon and dwell in peace in the land.

40.6.0.en: Gedaliah continued his words by saying that he would remain in Mizpah as a deputy for Babylon to meet the envoys of Nebuchadnezzar and pay him the tribute and all the reports required. As for them, he invited them to dwell in their cities where they had lived in the kingdom of Judah, and to cultivate the fields and gather fruits as they wished, of grapes, figs, olives and all the fruits of the field.

40.7.0.en: All the Jews who had fled to the countries surrounding the kingdom of Judah also heard of Gedaliah's appointment as governor amid a settled state of security and the return of normal life, so they returned to their land and began to cultivate their lands.

40.7.1.en: How beautiful it is to live in peace so that you can practice your spiritual life and enjoy God. So keep away from conflict with others as much as you can, and seek peace in order to devote yourself to life with God.

40.8.0.en: Some of the princes, that is, Jewish officers such as Johanan the son of Kareah, discovered a plot to assassinate Gedaliah the governor. This plot was an agreement between “Ishmael,” who was of the royal line, and “Baalis,” king of the Ammonites, to whom Ishmael had fled when Babylon attacked the kingdom of Judah. It appears that the aim of this plot was for the king of the Ammonites to take the kingdom of Judah and resist Babylon. So Johanan and those with him of the officers and soldiers came and told Gedaliah of the plot, but sadly he did not believe them and considered their words slander and false accusation. Thus Gedaliah rushed to judge by his own opinion and did not return to God in prayer or consult the prophet Jeremiah, who was staying beside him.

40.8.1.en: Take refuge in prayer in every matter that is presented to you, especially in great decisions, so that you hear His voice and He guides you and you keep yourself from the snares of the devil. God is near to you; He wants to lead your life in peace, so seek Him and persist before Him, and you will hear His voice.

40.9.0.en: Johanan had pity on Gedaliah and was concerned to preserve the land of Judah, which had begun to settle under Gedaliah's leadership. So he asked Gedaliah's permission to go and kill Ishmael, and thus deliver him from this plot.

40.10.0.en: Gedaliah rejected Johanan's counsel and accused him of lying. So he lost an opportunity sent to him by God for deliverance, because he relied on his own opinion. Perhaps he felt his strength when he became governor. Despite his piety, he was weak in this situation and was compelled to pay a costly price, which was his whole life.

40.10.1.en: The assassination of Gedaliah, governor of Judah
